solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Cash wanting as monstrous car eats petrol — that's taking the pee!

definitions.text: Cash wanting as monstrous car eats petrol — that's taking the pee!

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so the two letters of the next word are removed from the word before it

parts.note: taken as written, the letters removed

indicators.note: monstrous suggests something misshapen, so these letters are twisted into a new order
taking away 'the pee' means the letter P is removed from the fodder, with a nod to the slang for mockery

explanation.surface: A sneering remark about a gas-guzzling monster of a car: it is a joke at the owner's expense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cash wanting as' leaves CH. 'Monstrous' scrambles CAR EATS PETROL once 'taking the pee' has removed its P, giving ELSEATRACTOR. The whole clue is also the definition: a CHELSEA TRACTOR is a mocking British name for a big 4x4 SUV driven around posh parts of London.
explanation.definitionFit: The term is British mockery for a large off-road vehicle used only on smart city streets, a thirsty monster that is itself a jibe.

clue.text: Moscow gold?

definitions.meaning: Moscow is the chief city of Russia, an example of a seat of government
gold is wealth, money or assets used to fund enterprise; the question mark flags the example

explanation.surface: Seems to ask about Soviet treasure, the so-called Moscow gold.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface evokes the historical 'Moscow gold', but the two words are read separately.
explanation.definitionFit: Moscow is a seat of government, and gold is wealth or funds, both senses of the same word.

clue.text: Look in envy at our toy there, a ukulele starter set

indicators.note: set is read as the verb arrange, so the letters before it are put into a new order
a starter is the opening course, here the first letter of the instrument's name

explanation.surface: A child gloats over a new toy, a ukulele starter kit, inviting a friend to be jealous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set' looks like part of 'starter set', but it is the anagram signal for AT OUR TOY THERE A plus U, the start of 'ukulele'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is a taunting invitation for someone to be jealous of what the speaker has.

clue.text: Fill up half tank in Spain

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the assembled letters are read from bottom to top
in places the half word inside the letters for Spain

parts.note: ES is the international code for Spain

indicators.note: half takes the first two of the four letters of tank

explanation.surface: Filling the fuel tank halfway while driving in Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: TA, half of 'tank', goes 'in' ES to make ETAS, and 'up' turns that round. 'Fill up' looks like one phrase, but 'up' is the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To fill someone with food is to satisfy their appetite completely, a plain synonym.

clue.text: Short about an infectious disease including publicity

parts.note: an gives the indefinite article A

indicators.note: including means one piece holds another inside it

parts.note: pox is a general name for infectious diseases such as smallpox
PR stands for public relations, i.e. publicity

explanation.surface: Seems to describe a brief item about a contagious illness with publicity attached.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a description of the word itself: it is the shortened form of a word meaning 'about'.
explanation.definitionFit: The abbreviation is short for approximately, which means roughly or around.

clue.text: Blair torn over ironic comedy

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means the first piece sits above the second
torn means ripped apart, so the letters of the name are rearranged

parts.note: dry humour is ironic and understated

explanation.surface: Tony Blair is pulled apart in an ironic comedy sketch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Torn' rearranges BLAIR to RIBAL, which sits 'over' DRY.
explanation.definitionFit: Coarse, bawdy humour is a kind of comedy; the definition is broad but fair.

clue.text: What'll clean up pollution from vehicle emissions and black stuff around the ends of the earth

parts.note: a car is a vehicle
BO, body odour, is an unwelcome bodily emission
the ends of the earth are its poles, North and South, N and S
ink is black liquid used for writing

explanation.surface: Describes a green technology that cleans up exhaust fumes and soot from around the globe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The ends of the earth' looks like the letters E and H, but means the poles, N and S. 'Around' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A forest or ocean absorbing atmospheric carbon dioxide removes pollution, which is what this term names.

clue.text: After murder by space apes, now I've fashioned dagger, perhaps

parts.note: to off someone is slang for killing them
an en is a printing space half the width of an em

indicators.note: fashioned means shaped or made, so these letters are formed into a new order

explanation.surface: A sinister tale of apes in space who, after a killing, make themselves a dagger.
explanation.walkthrough: OFF and EN come first, then 'fashioned' rearranges APES NOW IVE. 'After' and 'by' are link words. To 'off' someone is US slang for murder.
explanation.definitionFit: A dagger is one example of a weapon carried to attack, as the legal phrase covers; hence 'perhaps'.

clue.text: Dome of copper mainly from the ends of the earth

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

indicators.note: mainly means most of it, so the last letter of the word is dropped

parts.words: from the ends of the earth
parts.note: polar means coming from the regions at the ends of the earth

explanation.surface: A copper-clad dome made from materials gathered from the far corners of the world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mainly' cuts the last letter from POLAR, leaving POLA.
explanation.definitionFit: A small rounded roof crowning a building is a synonym of the definition.

clue.text: Mine's principal source of replacement fuel

parts.note: a pit is a mine; with the 's it gives PITS
top means principal or chief

explanation.surface: Seems to claim that a coal mine is the main supplier of fuel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mine' looks like coal and fuel, but the fuel is a racing car's, taken on during a pause in the race.
explanation.definitionFit: In motor racing, a car calls in mid-race for new tyres and fuel, so this halt is where fresh fuel comes from.

clue.text: Migrant perhaps said to have travelled with disease

parts.note: a migrant may be a bird, such as a swallow that flies south

indicators.note: said to have signals that the next word is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: flew is the past tense of fly, to travel by air

explanation.surface: A migrant is suspected of bringing a disease with them on their travels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Migrant' suggests a person, but here it is a bird that migrates.
explanation.definitionFit: Avian influenza is an illness, so the definition is a general category.

clue.text: One to the left's wrong turn

indicators.note: turn means the word for wrong is spun round and read backwards

parts.note: a tort is a civil wrong in law

explanation.surface: Someone takes a wrong turn while heading left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrong turn' reads as a mistake in driving, but 'wrong' is the legal TORT, and 'turn' turns it round. 'One to the left' means a political leftist; the 's is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Short for Trotskyist, a follower of Trotsky and so a person on the far political left.

clue.text: Mean, inflamed spot and bit of fuzz, perhaps — teenager beginning to get old

parts.note: a boil is an inflamed spot on the skin
down is soft fine hair, such as a teenager's first fuzz

indicators.note: beginning picks out the opening letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: A teenager's spot and wispy fuzz are the start of growing up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mean' looks like an adjective about nastiness, but is the verb, as in 'amount to'.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means to amount to, or to signify at its core, so it can replace mean in a sentence.

clue.text: Power lunch is so drunken at overseas office

indicators.note: drunken means unsteady and reeling, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: P is the physics symbol for power

explanation.surface: A boozy power lunch at an embassy abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Power lunch' reads as one phrase, but 'Power' only gives P, mixed with LUNCH IS SO by 'drunken'.
explanation.definitionFit: The post of a diplomat representing a state in a foreign city is an office held abroad.

clue.text: Bacon's cubist piece in the Louvre?

definitions.text: Bacon's cubist piece in the Louvre?

parts.words: Bacon's cubist piece in the Louvre?
parts.note: the surface suggests a painting by Francis Bacon hanging in a Paris gallery, but it is a cube of bacon, named in French

explanation.surface: Seems to ask about a Cubist painting by the artist Francis Bacon in the Paris museum.
explanation.walkthrough: Francis Bacon was a British painter, and the Louvre is in Paris, so the clue points to a French word for a small cube of bacon.
explanation.definitionFit: The French culinary term is a small strip or cube of fatty pork, a cubist piece of bacon.

clue.text: Veggie family having fool and most of ice in two cups

indicators.note: in puts the middle pieces inside the garment with two cups

parts.note: a bra has two cups
an ass is a fool

indicators.note: most of means all but the last letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: A vegetarian family drinks two cups of something with fruit fool and ice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fool' and 'cups' suggest a dessert, but they are an ASS and a BRA. 'Most of' cuts ICE to IC. 'Having' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The cabbage genus, including broccoli and sprouts, is a family of vegetables in everyday terms.

clue.text: Stir wake at sea?

indicators.note: at sea means confused and all over the place, so the letters are muddled

explanation.surface: Stirring up a wake in the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At sea' rearranges STIR WAKE, and the whole clue also describes the sport.
explanation.definitionFit: Being towed on skis behind a speedboat churns the wake on the water, so the whole clue describes the sport.

clue.text: Following father back, I catch glimpse of Auntie's special bloomers

indicators.note: following means the next piece comes after the abbreviation for father

parts.note: Fr is the abbreviation for Father, a priest's title

indicators.note: back means the words I and catch are read from right to left

parts.note: to catch something can mean to see it

indicators.note: a glimpse is only a small part, so just the first letter is taken

explanation.surface: Behind Dad, someone catches sight of Auntie's special knickers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomers' looks like old-fashioned underwear, but means flowers. 'Back' turns I SEE into EESI, and 'glimpse of' takes A from 'Auntie'.
explanation.definitionFit: Scented garden flowers of the iris family are things that bloom, a cheeky crossword-style sense.

clue.text: Sting run by church

parts.note: to flee is to run away
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A wasp sting makes someone run to the church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sting' looks like an insect's attack, but it is slang for swindle. 'By' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are slang for cheating or overcharging someone, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Take in how truth's said to be commonly expressed

indicators.note: commonly expressed signals that the phrase is spoken and heard rather than spelt

parts.note: the saying goes that many a true word is spoken in jest, so truth is said in jest

explanation.surface: Reads like a remark about how proverbs put truth into words.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Commonly expressed' points both to the proverb 'many a true word is spoken in jest' and to speaking the phrase aloud.
explanation.definitionFit: To swallow food or absorb information is to take it into the body or mind.

clue.text: Prune plant climbing window ledge and frame

indicators.note: prune means cut back, so the last letter of the plant is trimmed off

parts.note: a tree is a plant

indicators.note: in a down clue, climbing means the word for ledge is read upwards

parts.note: a sill is a window ledge

explanation.surface: A gardener prunes a climbing plant on the window ledge and its supporting frame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prune' looks like a fruit or the definition, but cuts TREE to TRE. 'Climbing' turns SILL to LLIS.
explanation.definitionFit: A lattice of wood for climbing plants is a framework of crossing strips.

clue.text: Powerful holy man's not the first to sin

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for Saint, a holy man

indicators.note: not the first means the opening letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: to sin is to do wrong

explanation.surface: A powerful holy man is not the first to sin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not the first' drops the W from WRONG; 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Mighty and forceful, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Weird men, loners, collecting car model registrations

indicators.note: collecting means the rearranged letters gather in the next piece
weird means strange and out of shape, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

parts.note: the Model T was the famous Ford car

explanation.surface: Odd men and loners collect car models and register them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Weird' rearranges MEN LONERS, and 'collecting' takes T inside. 'Model' looks like a scale model, but is Ford's Model T.
explanation.definitionFit: Signing up students or members are acts of joining a register, so the two plurals match.

clue.text: Youth cutting male worker?

parts.note: he is a male pronoun

indicators.note: cutting means the final letter of the insect is cut off

parts.note: a worker bee is the classic crossword worker

explanation.surface: A young man is being cut out of the workforce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Youth' looks like a young person; it is the Greek goddess of youth.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth she is the goddess of youthful bloom, so she personifies the definition.

clue.text: Correct to keep going for now?

definitions.meaning: to correct a text is to revise it and fix its errors
to tide over means to keep someone going for the time being; the question mark says the word is to be read with 'over' as an instruction to write it backwards

explanation.surface: Asks whether correcting is just a way to keep things going for the moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To keep going for now' is the phrase TIDE OVER, read as an instruction: put TIDE over, i.e. reverse it.
explanation.definitionFit: To revise a text and fix its mistakes is a synonym for putting it right.

clue.text: Man in fool's garb

indicators.note: in places the pronoun for a man inside the other word

parts.note: a clot is a fool; the 's gives CLOTS
he is the pronoun for a man

explanation.surface: A man dressed in a jester's outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fool's garb' reads as motley, but 'fool's' gives CLOTS.
explanation.definitionFit: Garments and dress in general are what the old word garb means.

clue.text: I loved pa madly? Not very this then!

definitions.text: I loved pa madly? Not very this then!

indicators.note: madly means wildly, so the letters are rearranged
not means the abbreviation for very is left out of the fodder

explanation.surface: Someone admits to adoring their father, and is told that is not the famous complex then.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not very' removes V from I LOVED PA, and 'madly' rearranges what is left. The whole clue is the definition: the Oedipus complex is about loving the mother, not the father.
explanation.definitionFit: Freud's complex names a child's desire for the opposite-sex parent and rivalry with the father, so loving pa is not it.

clue.text: When crossing flowers, plant two feet down here, one after the other

definitions.text: When crossing flowers, plant two feet down here, one after the other

parts.words: When crossing flowers, plant two feet down here, one after the other
parts.note: flowers looks like garden blooms but means things that flow, rivers; to cross one you put your feet on these in turn

explanation.walkthrough: 'Flowers' wants to be garden plants and 'plant' a verb of gardening; in fact a flower is a river and you plant your feet.
explanation.definitionFit: A row of rocks in a stream lets a walker cross by setting one foot after the other on each.
